title: Fed Delivers First Rate Hike Since 2023 as Global Central Banks Tighten Together
content:
The window's defining event was the Fed delivering its first rate rise since 2023, confirming the pivot away from the summer's rate-cut narrative. Chair Kevin Warsh framed inflation as too high for too long, and a strong August payrolls print of **162,000** hardened the case.

After Warsh's late-August remarks turned September from a coin-flip into a near-certainty, futures priced about a **92%** chance of a move, and on 16 September the FOMC voted 12-0 to lift the funds rate to **3.75%-4%**. The dot plot leaned hawkish, signalling another hike before year-end; the ECB had already raised its deposit rate to **2.5%** on 10 September.

This **synchronised tightening** rippled across assets, firming front-end yields, supporting the dollar and pressuring rate-sensitive equities. With policy leaning against inflation on both sides of the Atlantic, the pace of further hikes became the market's central question.

title: Global Long-End Bond Rout Deepens on Rising Term Premium and Fiscal Strain
content:
Running beneath the policy story was a worldwide sell-off in long-dated government debt, as investors demanded a higher **term premium** for heavy issuance, sticky inflation and fading central-bank support. The long end led the move, a theme that reinforced week after week.

The US 10-year briefly touched **5%** intraday and printed its highest level since 2023, while the 2-year reached a multi-month peak. The strain was global: Japan's 10-year cleared **3%** for the first time since 1996, and the UK's 30-year gilt sat near **5.88%**, with French debt near multi-year highs on fiscal worries.

The rout mattered because higher long yields lift discount rates everywhere, pressuring equities, housing and credit, and signalling that fiscal as much as monetary forces now steer the curve. Auctions and supply remained the swing factor to watch.

title: Middle East Oil Shock Keeps Crude Elevated and Reinforces Inflation Fears
content:
The causal spark linking the window's themes was a Middle East oil shock, as the US-Iran conflict and threats around the Strait of Hormuz drove a broad **supply shock**. Fears over the world's most important chokepoint kept a persistent risk premium in crude.

Brent pushed above **$104** and WTI settled near **$102**, with US crude advancing more than **18%** over the month and climbing for six straight sessions at the peak. Saudi Arabia's rerouting of exports through Hormuz to offset a pipeline closure later eased some of the pressure, but the tension lingered.

The shock mattered because it fed directly into inflation prints and central-bank rhetoric, with both Warsh and Lagarde citing energy, hardening the case for higher rates and higher yields. Any renewed Hormuz disruption stayed the key tail risk.

title: AI Equity Leadership Splits Between Chipmakers and Hyperscalers
content:
US equity leadership fractured within the AI complex itself. After indices set records early in the window, the rate repricing exposed a new fault line between chipmakers dependent on relentless **AI capex** and hyperscalers that could profit by trimming it.

In the week of the hike Nvidia fell more than **3%** while Meta, Microsoft and Alphabet advanced, and the S&P 500 slipped to around **7,646** as higher yields weighed on the richest multiples. Narrow breadth left benchmarks unusually hostage to a handful of megacap names.

The divergence mattered because it questioned the single-trade dominance of the AI rally just as discount rates rose. With Nvidia still the market's largest directional force, the durability of AI earnings against a tightening Fed became the key test into the fourth quarter.
